articleTitle: Intrinsic safety-simplicity itself
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Safety in Hazardous Areas
abstract: The author shows that making an electrical system easier to apply will make a safer system. This premise is based upon the fact that if a set of rules is easily applied, then people will use it. Intrinsic safety offers the highest level of safety of all the explosion-protection techniques. It also offers a high level of personal safety since it uses low voltage, typically less than 30 volts, low current, usually less then 250 mA and low powers, of the order of 0.5 watts. Since this technique uses such low power levels and components that are substantially derated, then obviously, the equipment must be highly reliable.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Interaction of lightning and other high power surges with intrinsically safe installations
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Safety in Hazardous Areas
abstract: It is demonstrated that heavy current surges from faults in power electrical equipment and lightning can theoretically create a transient problem in intrinsically safe circuits. It is argued that in a well bonded plant with adequate power and lightning earths then in Zone 1 and 2 this slight transient risk is acceptable as existing installations demonstrate. In the particular case of Zone 0, acceptance of the German requirement for galvanic isolation is advocated for the usual risk, and where there is a high potential risk of severe transient potential voltages then a more elaborate configuration similar to Dutch practice is commended. It is believed that these proposals are a practical compromise and might remove one major obstacle to creating a uniform European Code of Practice.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Incendivity of electrical sparking due to circulating currents in the enclosures of large electrical machines
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Safety in Hazardous Areas
abstract: An explosion occurred within an electric motor on an off-shore platform in late 1985. It is considered that this ignition could have been the result of electrical sparking at the joints of the motor enclosure, due to circulating currents. The authors show that where circulating currents are interrupted by discontinuities at joints in the current path, arcing or sparking can occur which may be incendive, despite the very low voltages involved. The energy available for ignition depends upon the inductance of the current path and the magnitude of the circulating current. Test results indicate that in machines of interest, the effective inductance of the current path is typically 1 mu H to 2 mu H.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Complications from the interaction between EEC directives, European standards for explosion safety and the equivalent national standards
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Safety in Hazardous Areas
abstract: Increasingly in most European countries the majority of designs of electrical apparatus and instrumentation for potentially explosive atmospheres comply with the European Standards (ENs) for explosion safety. The Standards are referred to in the relevant EEC Directives intended to allow unimpeded movement between EEC countries. There are numerous complications which in varying degrees can result in problems which the Directives are intended in principle to overcome. The more significant of these complexities are reviewed and tentative suggestions are made for dealing with the problems with a cautious eye on 1992.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The safety of optical systems in flammable atmospheres
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Safety in Hazardous Areas
abstract: Since the very first use of optical systems in the process industries there has been a tacit assumption that, because they are not electrical, they do not present an ignition risk when used in flammable atmospheres. The author describes the results obtained from experimental work. He draws conclusions about an optical ignition mechanism and whether there is sufficient of an ignition risk for precautions to be advisable when optical systems are used in flammable atmospheres. The results obtained suggest that radiation intensities of 1*10/sup 5/ to 4*10/sup 5/ W/m/sup 2/ and above are ignition capable. Modern fibre optic systems are capable of radiation intensities of 10/sup 8/ W/m/sup 2/. The ignition mechanism requires the radiation to be absorbed by a small solid object which is thus raised to a high temperature.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Ex.o. Oil filling for control and instrumentation circuits and apparatus
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Safety in Hazardous Areas
abstract: The use of oil filling as a protection technique for electrical apparatus to be used in hazardous areas has been established for many years. Oil filling has some interesting and useful properties, and it is worth considering its application for low powered apparatus. The author outlines the technique, discusses its advantages and shows how it may be applied to apparatus such as remote outstations of distributed control systems which are low current apparatus and do not have normally arcing or sparking parts.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Plastics casings for the type of protection 'flameproof enclosure d'
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Safety in Hazardous Areas
abstract: In explosive atmospheres, electrical components which, during operation, constitute potential ignition sources (due for example to their high surface temperature or a spark at break) must be installed in a casing of the type of protection 'flameproof enclosure d'. This casing must both withstand and explosion on the inside and be flameproof. For many years, the manufacturers of electrical equipment have used plastics for flameproof casings of small volume. Due the the specific stressing of the material at higher volumes, however, the standard characteristics available for the design are not sufficient. The authors therefore develop a specific test method which allows the influence of the main risks on strength and fracture behaviour of different types of plastics to be determined. The results of the test are intended to be a help in selecting the material and the wall thickness of the casing.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Which 'type of protection' (electrical equipment safety)
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Safety in Hazardous Areas
abstract: When electrical equipment has to be installed in a hazardous area it must be prevented from igniting the flammable gas with which it may be in contact. There are currently seven internationally agreed 'Types of Protection' available to the manufacturer or user for this purpose together with several other methods not necessarily acceptable outside the country of certification. The author examines the applications and limitations of each protection type which should enable the user to eliminate the unsuitable types of protection. Each type of protection has its limitations (e.g. electrical, physical or financial) and some research is usually necessary before an optimal system is arrived at.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Developments in systems engineering in UK coal mines
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Safety in Hazardous Areas
abstract: Recent changes to the UK mining industry have presented new and more demanding problems to all engineering disciplines both within and supplying the industry. Against thick backcloth, the author identifies how the development and application of systems technology has contributed towards improvements in efficiency and productivity whilst maintaining high standards of safety in the use of electrical equipment in a hazardous environment.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Reducing explosion risks by new techniques-results of recent investigations by BVS
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Safety in Hazardous Areas
abstract: WBK-BVS in Dortmund is the only authorized testing station in West Germany for firedamp and dust explosion protection of group II (surface) equipment. In addition to testing and certification activities, and collaboration in national and international committees for the unification of standards, research work is also carried out. In this paper, the authors present some of the results of this research.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Inspection, maintenance and testing of electrical equipment for use in potentially explosive atmospheres
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Safety in Hazardous Areas
abstract: Electrical apparatus for use in potentially explosive atmospheres is specially constructed, tested and certified to reduce the risk that it could be the source of an incendive spark. It has built into it physical features which make it acceptable for use in areas classified as having potentially explosive atmospheres. In an ideal world, once the equipment has been installed correctly it would stay that way forever. Unfortunately, in practice, equipment is subject to corrosion, vibration, accidental damage and a dozen other factors which affect its integrity. It is, therefore, necessary to ensure that the features provided to obviate the creation of ignition (capable sparks or hot surfaces) are maintained in a satisfactory condition. The authors describe an inspection system which records any faults found, plus any subsequent repairs. By analysing the numbers and types of faults found the effectiveness of the inspection system, and the suitability of the apparatus, can be monitored.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Italian experience on hazardous area classification and selection of electrical installations and apparatus in industrial plants
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Safety in Hazardous Areas
abstract: The authors give an outline of the Italian Standards relevant to hazardous area classifications and selection of safety electrical equipment and of the present technical trends in this field. Further considerations are reported, resulting from CESI experience in the activities of area classification, verifications on plants and laboratory testing on safety equipment. In this connection particular attention is paid to the problem of the evaluation of the safety level of electrical plants in hazardous areas during their operating life. To this purpose the verification of compliance of aged equipment with safety standard may be necessary.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The education of installation personnel (dealing with the biggest risk)
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Safety in Hazardous Areas
abstract: The author believes that the greatest potential danger for industries who use electrical equipment in potentially explosive atmospheres, is the ignorance of installation personnel. The author presents examples which support this view, based on extensive experience of on-site inspection and audits of explosion protected electrical equipment, during which numerous items of equipment have been found in an unsafe condition. In nearly every instance, the danger could have been avoided if the installer or maintainer had had the most basic understanding of safety features incorporated in the equipment.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Certification of inverter-fed induction motors for use in hazardous areas
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Safety in Hazardous Areas
abstract: The use of variable speed drive motors fed from static frequency converters is increasing generally by approximately 30% per annum. To facilitate their use in hazardous areas, a thorough study is required of the appropriate safety requirements so that relevant safety standards can be updated and acceptable and convenient procedures developed. The authors present a certification of invertor-fed induction motors for use in hazardous areas.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The safe gap: effect of explosion pressure
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Safety in Hazardous Areas
abstract: Flame-proof enclosure is one method of preventing accidental ignition of a flammable atmosphere by sparking in an electrical apparatus. Transmission of the explosion from inside the apparatus to the external atmosphere is prevented if the gap between plain parallel flange surfaces is less than the maximum experimental safe gap (MESG). In practice flange gaps permitted in electrical apparatus are less than the MESG to allow a factor of safety. The essential features of the safe gap and the MESG are reproduced and the effect of explosion pressure is looked at.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Intrinsic safety reference curves: some recent considerations
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Safety in Hazardous Areas
abstract: Both the CENELEC and IEC Standards dealing with intrinsic safety contain reference curves which are essentially the same as the minimum igniting current and voltage curves presented by Widginton in 1968. The validity of some of these curves, particularly those for capacitive circuits, has been questioned. In 1974 IEC Sub-Committee SC31-G 'Intrinsic safety' set up a Working Group, WG2 'Ignition data'. The author indicates what progress has so far been made by the WG, and also provides some information on reference curves for high-voltage resistive circuits, a subject outside the WG's remit.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Electrical safety in hazardous locations-Canadian Federal Enterprises
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Safety in Hazardous Areas
abstract: The use of electrical equipment in hazardous locations will always cause problems. The problems which arise are due to ignitable dusts and gases in the same place as sparks. In the Federal Enterprises of Canada, the industries with these problems are generally coal mining, grain storage and gas and oil. The author discusses safety in these locations.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Multi-way explosion protected junction and marshalling boxes
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Safety in Hazardous Areas
abstract: A power limit concept is described for the assessment and, where necessary, testing of multi-way junction and marshalling boxes protected by any of the established protection concepts. The power limit concept results in severe limitation of the maximum permissible numbers of terminal ways compared with earlier methods of safety assessment, because it must be assumed that terminals will be operated at their maximum ratings. Where terminals are operated below their ratings, and where diversity applies, significant relaxations can be achieved which the concept allows to be calculated. Appropriate guidance on achieving these relaxations should be given in future codes of practice.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Could detection provide a dynamic path to the safe use of electrical equipment in hazardous areas?
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Safety in Hazardous Areas
abstract: All industrial complexes producing or using flammable gases have a background concentration gas present. The author looks at detection of gas which could lead to an alarm system activated when there is too much gas. This technique could mean the safe use of electrical equipment in hazardous areas.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Safety requirements for analytical instruments
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Safety in Hazardous Areas
abstract: In a hazardous environments made dangerous by flammable gases precautions can include continuous provision of air to dilute the flammable gas to safe concentrations. The authors describes the continuous dilution requirements in terms both of principle and of detail, and illustrate why requirements are likely to become progressively more detailed to cover the various types of instrument involved. In view of the increasing complexity, proposals are made for simplifications of the approach that may be considered both by the supplier and the user of the equipment.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The specification, testing and application of flameproof and increased safety electrical enclosures for use in hazardous atmospheres
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Safety in Hazardous Areas
abstract: Any plant involving the processing of flammable mixtures, liquids and gases has to have an area classification undertaken in order that the risk zones can be properly assigned. Once this has been carried out, the project then passes to the design team which embraces all disciplines. The author explains the significant of the specification, testing and application of flameproof electrical safety enclosures for use in hazardous atmospheres.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Cells and batteries in hazardous areas: problems and solutions
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Safety in Hazardous Areas
abstract: There is increasing interest in the use of cells and batteries in hazardous areas. The interest ranges across all types of electrochemical systems currently available commercially, and all sized from small individual cells for microcomputer memory support to substantial stand-by battery power supplies. Traditionally batteries have been located in nonhazardous areas wherever possible, but this is becoming less attractive for technical and economic reasons. The author shows that is is therefore necessary to consider the requirements that should apply for safety in hazardous areas.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Standards-towards change (mining safety)
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Safety in Hazardous Areas
abstract: British Coal is continually pursuing improvements in safety, reliability and productivity. This often results in the introduction of new technology, apparatus and systems, and, increasingly more so today, using the technical expertise gained both in Europe and the rest of the world. Engineers, to achieve these goals, are using the many forms of protection techniques available for mining applications. The author reviews past and current practices and examines future trends that may permit the introduction of new designs of protection apparatus and systems more readily.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Gas studied in lead acid batteries
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Safety in Hazardous Areas
abstract: A modern coal mine would be unrecognisable to a miner from the turn of the century, and the lead acid battery has made its contribution to the improved conditions now prevailing underground. Whilst the use of lead acid batteries has brought benefits they do themselves constitute a risk, albeit a small one, in hazardous areas. These risks have, in the past, been associated with arcing and with hydrogen evolution. The authors seek to show how progress in battery technology may introduce a hitherto unconsidered risk associated with the retention of flammable atmospheres inside the battery itself.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The evolution of the modern gate end box
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Safety in Hazardous Areas
abstract: Electricity was introduced into collieries during the late 19th Century and grew rapidly from powering small pumps to conveyors and coal cutting equipment. It was quickly realised however, that the introduction of electricity into hazardous areas was also a potential means of igniting methane. It was also recognised that switchgear to be used in coal mines would, in addition to being mechanically robust, require to be flameproof. The author shows how the design of the gate end box enclosure has changed quite dramatically over the years, from the tall rectangular structure of the 1930s to the modern cubic structure. He also shows that modern enclosures have hinged single bolt fixing front covers allowing easy access to the contactor compartment.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Training for competence in hazardous area equipment maintenance
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Safety in Hazardous Areas
abstract: Area classification is an essential activity to prevent the ignition of an explosive gas atmosphere by apparatus as its physical condition and performance tend to deteriorate due to age, environmental attack and constant use. In particular, National Standards and Codes of Practice require that the personnel who undertake these tasks are competent to do so by virtue of the training they have received. The author shows the the response to the need for trained personnel has encouraged the active support of an initiative in the UK to establish a nationally recognised training certificate for personnel who work on electrical and instrumentation equipment for use in hazardous atmospheres.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Certification to harmonised standards: a manufacturer's viewpoint
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Safety in Hazardous Areas
abstract: Electrical installations must be safe and in order to maximise their international acceptability it is desirable to obtain product type-certification to European standards. The authors believe that in the development of international standards conflicts have been created due to different national practices. These problems are considered.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Aspects of temperature rise measurement and temperature protection of rotating electrical machines, with particular reference to increased safety motors and operation at variable speed
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Safety in Hazardous Areas
abstract: Guaranteeing that the temperature of apparatus installed in a hazardous area does not rise to a level which would cause ignition of the hazardous gas/air mixture is a vital part of all the protection concepts. The author reviews some aspects of temperature measurement and control relating to rotating electrical machines. The aspects are looked at particularly from the point of view of satisfying the certifying authority that they are justified in issuing a certificate confirming compliance with one of the relevant standards.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Investigation of explosions in a number of Ex-certified handlamps and an examination of relevant safety standards
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Safety in Hazardous Areas
abstract: Over a period of less than two years five handlamps of the same type have exploded. In each case the front end of the lamp blew off, fortunately injuring no one and causing little damage. The handlamps were properly manufactured and correctly certified to UK and European Standards that indicated that they were safe for use in flammable atmospheres (including hydrogen). The authors describe the incidents and their investigation. They also discuss some of the constructional requirements of the standards and how they relate to these incidents.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Electrical safety of process instrumentation in areas with potentially explosive gas atmospheres
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Safety in Hazardous Areas
abstract: Many European installation rules (including DIN 57 165/VDE 0165, BS 5345, NE 3410) on electrical systems in areas with potentially explosive gas atmospheres are generally in line with the recommendations of publication IEC 79-14 with regard to selection of the recommended type of protection. These recommendations also apply to electronic process instrumentation. Process instruments are often unavoidably in contact with this atmosphere so they must be contained. The author looks at the safety of these instruments.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
